rules.title: The least code that solves the problem
rules.what: Write the least code that solves the stated problem. No speculative generality, no second caller that does not exist, no framework for a script.
rules.why: Every line is written, reviewed, tested, loaded, executed and carried through every future migration. Volume is the easiest thing to mistake for progress.
rules.how: When about to generalise, name the second caller. With no answer, write the specific version. Prefer deleting to abstracting.

verify.how: Diff review: added abstractions each name their second caller or are removed.

limits: Applied at the margin; refactoring towards less code is encouraged, rewriting everything is not.

rules.title: Prefer the simplest solution
rules.what: Prefer the simplest architecture that meets the need: monolith before microservices, single region before multi-region, one service before a distributed system.
rules.why: Distributed architectures multiply runtimes, network hops, observability and failure modes. Each unit of scale must be paid for by a measured need.
rules.how: Start simple, and split only when a measured limit (latency, load, team size) demands it. Record the measurement that justified the split.

verify.how: Architecture decisions cite the measured constraint that ruled out the simpler option.

limits: Organisational constraints (team boundaries) are legitimate reasons; state them as such.

rules.title: Size resources to the real load
rules.what: Size every runtime (instances, containers, functions, queues, caches) to the measured or evidenced load, with headroom stated as a number.
rules.why: Oversized infra burns resources 24/7 whether or not anyone uses the service; undersized infra fails on the first peak. Only the measured load can arbitrate.
rules.how: Right-size from real metrics, use autoscaling where the load varies, and document the headroom assumption ('2x the observed p95').

verify.how: Resource sizing traceable to observed metrics; utilisation reviewed against them.

limits: Serverless shifts sizing to the provider; the rule then applies to limits and concurrency settings.

rules.title: Bound a function before you scale it
rules.what: A unit of work (function, job, request handler) has stated limits: timeout, max input size, max fan-out. Make it correct once before replicating it.
rules.why: Scaling an unbounded function multiplies its worst case by the number of instances. Bounds are cheaper to add before the first autoscaling event than after.
rules.how: Declare timeout and size limits at the entry point; fail fast when exceeded; test the limit paths.

verify.how: A test exercises the limit path (oversized input, timeout) and gets a clean failure.

rules.title: Do not chain functions where one would do
rules.what: Avoid pipeline chains of managed functions or services where a single unit would do the same work.
rules.why: Each hop in a chain is a network round trip, a serialisation, a cold start and a new failure mode. Chains of small functions can multiply a task's cost while looking tidy.
rules.how: Merge steps that always run together; keep separation only where it isolates different scaling needs or failure domains.

verify.how: Pipeline steps each justify their separation by scaling or failure-domain needs.

limits: Legitimate for genuinely different scaling profiles; the rule targets fashion-driven splitting.

rules.title: Cache with explicit keys, TTLs and purge limits
rules.what: Every cache declares its key space, its TTL and its purge policy; bounded in size; invalidation documented at the point of creation.
rules.why: An unbounded cache with no invalidation is a slow leak: it grows until it OOMs, and it serves stale data that someone then debugs. Caching without bounds trades compute for memory forever.
rules.how: State key composition, TTL and max size next to the cache definition; document what invalidates it and what happens on purge.

patterns.note: Unbounded dict/object cache with no TTL; check eviction policy.

verify.how: Tests cover hit, miss, expiry and max size eviction.

limits: Cache efficiency must be measured (hit rate) to prove the trade-off; NR-MEASURE-002.

rules.title: Sober environments and CI
rules.what: Development, test and staging environments are sized, cleaned and shut down like production: no orphaned environments, no CI job that runs longer than it must.
rules.why: Idle environments run 24/7 for zero user value. CI waste compounds: every push times every job times every branch.
rules.how: TTL on preview environments, cancel superseded CI runs, keep build caches bounded, prefer incremental pipelines (rebuild what changed).

verify.how: Environment inventory shows creation date, owner, cost; CI config shows cancel-in-progress and bounded caches.

rules.title: Minimise and justify dependencies
rules.what: Every dependency must justify itself: what it saves, what it costs (size, supply-chain surface, maintenance), and whether a platform-native API suffices.
rules.why: A dependency is code you ship but do not read: it inflates bundles, extends build times and widens the attack surface. Whole libraries for one function are the common case, not the exception.
rules.how: Before adding: check for a native API, count what you actually use, and prefer the smaller alternative. Review the dependency list for orphans at each release.

patterns.note: Known-heavy libraries with platform-native or lighter alternatives; verify usage volume first.

verify.how: Each dependency entry has a use count in the codebase and a stated reason; unused ones removed.

limits: Well-used heavy libraries are legitimate; the rule targets one-function imports and dead weight.

rules.title: Design to last
rules.what: Favour choices that extend the service's life and the code's maintainability: quality code, tested, readable, documented decisions.
rules.why: A service that is cheap to run but impossible to maintain gets rewritten, and the rewrite costs more than the maintenance ever would. Durability is a resource decision.
rules.how: Test what matters, keep the code readable for a newcomer, record architectural decisions (date, context, trade-off) where the next reader finds them.

verify.how: Tests pass, decisions are recorded, a newcomer can navigate the entry points.

limits: Readability is not measurable; the reviewable artefact is the presence of tests and recorded decisions.
